description:
Hello there! 
I'm just someone who loves exploring technology, nerding out over space, and figuring out how things work. I'm into cybersecurity, AI, and building things just to see what's possible. A little nerdy, endlessly curious, and always up for a challenge.

Welcome to CITADEL — fellow Earthlings and potential extraterrestrials alike! 👽
summary:
NASA has recorded active fires from space since 2000. MODIS detects fire at 1 km resolution; its successor, VIIRS, sees at 375 m and finds more small fires. Join their records without correction and fire activity can appear to jump when the instrument changes. With MODIS ageing, decades of fire history risk losing their comparability.

KELVIN bridges this gap. It maps NASA FIRMS detections from five satellites onto a global 1 km equal-area grid, counting active cell-days. VIIRS is calibrated to MODIS over their 2012–2021 overlap, by region and season, with bootstrap uncertainty and leave-one-year-out validation. A mathematical screening score flags potential false alarms, including industrial heat. Users can select any region with available data to explore burning calendars, anomalies and historical trends. Its globally applicable framework supports meaningful long-term comparison.

We showcased KELVIN at NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 Ahmedabad, where ISRO SAC specialists shared valuable scientific insights. Our crop-residue burning case study demonstrated how harmonization reveals recurring seasonal patterns and unusual fire activity.

Fire Jukebox is where harmonization meets sonification. Satellite observations become sound, allowing users to hear sensor-induced discontinuities and how calibration reduces them. This opens Earth science to blind and low-vision users, students and anyone who learns by ear.

KELVIN keeps Earth's fire history continuous and open to everyone.
details:
KELVIN: EARTH'S HEAT, MEASURED FROM ORBIT

Team CITADEL,

THE STORY BEHIND KELVIN

Since 2000, NASA instruments in orbit have kept a running record of where the planet burns. For anyone studying fire, that record is precious, because the question "is this season unusual?" can only be answered against decades of earlier seasons. But a long record is only as good as its consistency, and this one has a flaw that comes from progress.

The record was started by MODIS, flying on Terra and Aqua, which detects active fire at about 1 km. It has been carried forward by VIIRS, on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, which detects at 375 m and finds many fires MODIS cannot; NASA's VIIRS 375 m user guide notes this higher sensitivity to small fires. The satellites also cross a place at different local times, and the fleet keeps growing. Join the two records without correction and fire activity jumps in the year the instrument changed. Nothing changed on the ground. Anyone reading the raw series would believe fire had increased, and have no way to know they were reading the sensor.

This is a global problem, because every country and every fire regime sits inside the same archive, and it is becoming urgent. MODIS is ageing, and the orbits of Terra and Aqua have drifted from their original overpass times since about 2022. The instrument that anchors the longest satellite fire record is the one fading out. We asked what it would take for that history to stay usable, comparable and trusted when someone reads it twenty years from now. KELVIN is our answer.

FROM A SCIENTIFIC CHALLENGE TO A REAL-WORLD DEMONSTRATION

We built KELVIN for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge "MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" and took it to the Ahmedabad local event. We presented and demonstrated it to specialists from ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC), and the technical discussions that followed were among the most valuable hours of the project. They shared scientific perspectives and insights on how reliable a satellite hotspot record really is, where its honest limits lie, how our approach could be strengthened, and how a tool like KELVIN could be used in the real world.

That conversation shaped how we describe and keep refining KELVIN. It is why uncertainty is drawn beside every harmonized value, why we keep detection confidence apart from a confirmed fire, why unfinished months are compared only with the same days of earlier years, and why we say plainly what our screening model can and cannot claim. It also pushed us to think past one country and one fire type, towards the global design described here. The mentors discussed and advised. The work and any errors are the team's own, and no endorsement by NASA or ISRO is implied. For us, the lesson was that a scientific tool improves when it is placed in front of experts and questioned.

THE CASE WE SHOWED: FIRES SET BY FARMERS

For the demonstration we chose a problem that returns to India every year: crop-residue, or stubble, burning. After harvest, farmers deliberately set fire to leftover straw to clear their fields quickly. These are human-induced fires, repeated season after season, and the public question is always the same: is this year worse than the last?

The case is hard for a satellite record, for a reason that makes it ideal for KELVIN. These fires are small and short-lived, which is exactly the kind of fire VIIRS sees and MODIS often misses. This is where the two sensors disagree most. Without correction, the newer satellites make the past look quieter than it was and the present look worse than it is.

KELVIN shows this in the product in four steps. A user draws the farming region on the map. The harmonized calendar places every year on one scale, so the burning season appears as a recurring band, month after month, year after year. The season view identifies the window that holds most of a year's activity, and the anomaly classes rank each month against the same month in earlier years, from record low to record high. Where the current month is not finished, KELVIN compares it only with the same days of earlier years, which matters because the burning season crosses month boundaries. The "raw stitch" line, a grey line of MODIS followed by raw VIIRS, shows the false jump that harmonization removes, so a viewer sees both the misleading version and the corrected one. The briefing then states the finding in plain language, with its caveats.

In this way KELVIN helps tell a genuine change in recorded fire activity from a change in the instrument. It does not attribute any detection to a person or a field, and a hotspot cell-day is a sign of active burning from space, not a count of farmers' fires.

THE SAME METHOD, ANYWHERE ON EARTH

Nothing in KELVIN depends on a country. The grid is global and the input is NASA FIRMS, which covers the whole planet. Crop-residue burning in Asia, forest-floor and peatland fires in the Indo-Pacific, savanna burning, and wildfires in the western United States all sit in the same archive, with different vegetation, climate and fire seasons. Because the correction factor is estimated for each place and season, KELVIN adapts to those differences, and its uncertainty bands show where the evidence is thin. Processing a new region is a matter of loading its FIRMS data.

Wildfire in California shows a very different fire world, driven by dry vegetation, wind and drought rather than farming. Here we are careful about early warning. Dry vegetation, fuel conditions and a place's historical pattern can indicate that conditions favour fire, and a detection that appears earlier in the season than the record would suggest can be an early sign that vegetation is already dry enough to burn. These are three different things, and KELVIN keeps them apart. A genuine fire detection is a thermal observation made by a satellite. A potential false alarm is a detection that the screening model scores as unlikely to be vegetation burning. An environmental warning sign is context, such as dry fuel, that raises the likelihood of fire without being a fire. A risk indicator is never presented as a confirmed detection. KELVIN measures burning that has already begun, and we do not claim validated prediction.

THE MATHEMATICS BEHIND KELVIN

Every equation below answers one question that a careful scientist would ask.

How do we compare a 1 km sensor with a 375 m one? We stop counting pixels and count places. Each detection at longitude λ and latitude φ is mapped to an equal-area cell:

x = R · λ · cos φ, y = R · φ, R = 6,371,007.181 m

cell = ( floor(x / 1000), floor(y / 1000) )

Because the projection preserves area, one cell means the same ground area at every latitude, so counts can be compared across the globe. We then define the active cell-day for a sensor family s:

A_s(c, d) = 1 if at least one detection from s falls in cell c on day d, otherwise 0

A fire that produces four VIIRS pixels and one MODIS pixel is one active cell-day for both, and several overpasses in a day collapse to one. This removes most of the resolution and overpass difference before any calibration, which is why we count cell-days and not raw detections.

How much is one VIIRS cell-day worth in MODIS terms? We measure it where both flew. For a 1-degree block b and season q, over February 2012 to December 2021,

k(b, q) = Σ A_MODIS(c, d) / Σ A_VIIRS(c, d)

with the sums running over every cell-day in the block and season. MODIS here means Terra or Aqua, and VIIRS is Suomi NPP, because Aqua and Suomi NPP cross at the same 13:30 local time and so sample the same part of the daily burning cycle. The window ends in 2021 on purpose: after about 2022 MODIS overpass times drift, and calibrating on those years would blend an orbit change into k. A ratio of sums is used instead of an average of ratios because it behaves well for count data with Poisson-like noise. Months more than three robust standard deviations from the block median are trimmed first. NOAA-20 is chained to Suomi NPP, and NOAA-21 to NOAA-20, by the same ratio over each pair's overlap, so the series continues as new satellites arrive.

What if a place has little evidence? One factor for the planet would be wrong, because sensitivity depends on fire size and type, which vary by place and season. A factor from a handful of cells would be noise. We blend the two with shrinkage:

k_level = w · r_level + (1 − w) · k_parent, w = N / (N + n0), n0 = 400

where r_level is the ratio observed at that level, N is the number of VIIRS cell-days behind it, and k_parent is the next broader estimate. The fall-back runs from block and season to block, then 10-degree tile, then the whole world. The more evidence a place has, the more it speaks for itself, and the level used is recorded and shown.

How sure are we? We resample the calibration years, not the months, 300 times, refit the whole hierarchy each time, and take the 5th and 95th percentiles of k as a 90 percent interval. Years are resampled because months within a year are not independent. The interval is carried into the series as

[ k_low · A_VIIRS , k_high · A_VIIRS ]

and drawn as a shaded band, so no harmonized value appears without its uncertainty.

How do we put it together? The harmonized series is

H(t) = A_MODIS(t) for dates before 1 January 2022

H(t) = k(b, q) · A_VIIRS(t) from then on

MODIS and VIIRS are never added, because in the overlap they see the same fires. The first 21 months of the record, when Terra flew alone, are corrected with a factor Σ(Terra or Aqua) / Σ Terra, learned from the following years and flagged as estimated.

How do we know it works? We hide one year at a time. For each year y, the factors are refitted without it and used to predict that year's MODIS from VIIRS. We report

WAPE = Σ | prediction − observed | / Σ observed

bias = Σ prediction / Σ observed − 1

together with R-squared and the Spearman rank correlation. This is out-of-sample evidence from real NASA data. On the first regions we fetched, which serve as demonstration and validation cases and not as the boundary of the platform, monthly out-of-sample error was about 13 percent, and the several-fold gap between raw VIIRS and MODIS fell to within about 2 percent of parity. We also run a synthetic known-answer test in which the pipeline must recover a planted factor within 6 percent. That test shows the code is correct. It says nothing about real-world accuracy and we never use it that way.

Is this month unusual? For each month we compare the value x with the same calendar month in earlier complete years:

ratio = x / median(baseline)

percentile = share of baseline years at or below x

z = ( x − median ) / ( 1.4826 · MAD )

The median and the median absolute deviation (MAD) are used because fire records are skewed and a few extreme years would distort a mean and standard deviation. The constant 1.4826 makes the MAD comparable to a standard deviation. A month outside the range of at least five baseline years is a record. Trends use the Theil-Sen slope with a Mann-Kendall test, which assume neither a straight line nor normal errors, and are reported as a tendency with caveats.

OUR DIFFERENTIATOR: SEPARATING FIRE FROM NOISE

A hotspot is not always a fire. Satellites also record sun glint, hot bare ground, gas flares, industrial furnaces, volcanoes and, now and then, plumes displaced from their source. Crop-residue fires are small, deliberate and brief. Wildfires are large, spreading and persistent. Industrial heat sources are small, steady and recurring. A tool that treats them alike will draw wrong conclusions from all three. Most hotspot tools show every detection; KELVIN asks how consistent each one is with real burning.

It screens in two layers. The first is rule-based and uses what NASA FIRMS already provides: low-confidence detections are dropped by default, with nominal and high-confidence settings available; the product's type field removes volcanoes, gas flares and offshore sources; duplicate rows are collapsed; and near-real-time rows give way to science-quality rows when those arrive.

The second is a mathematical screening score S between 0 and 1 for each cell-day:

S = σ( w1·a + w2·p + w3·q + w4·f + w5·u − b ), σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z))

where a is agreement between sensors on the same cell and day, p is the spatial and temporal persistence of activity in neighbouring cells and adjacent days, q is the detection confidence class, f is the fire radiative power relative to the area's own history, and u measures how unusual the activity is at that location compared with its own past years. A cell that glows every year at the same intensity is a probable static source, so u is low. The weights w and offset b set the balance of evidence. A single isolated low-power detection from one sensor at a place that glows every year scores low. A persistent, spreading detection seen by both sensors scores high. Users can set a minimum score and see the series recompute, so the effect of screening is never hidden.

What the model is and is not: it is a transparent, adjustable statistical estimate of how consistent a detection is with vegetation burning. It is not independent confirmation of any single fire. Detection confidence, which NASA assigns to each pixel, and a confirmed fire event, verified on the ground or by another source, are different things, and a high score does not turn one into the other. The weights are documented defaults. Validating them against independent fire records is part of our planned work, and until it is done we claim only that the screening is principled and visible, not that its accuracy is proven. An off-season guard also flags ratios built from only a handful of detections, so "twelve times the median" from three small fires is never presented as an alarm.

FIRE JUKEBOX: GIVING EARTH'S FIRE HISTORY A VOICE

NASA's Earth Jukebox challenge asks how Earth Information Center visualizations can be made accessible through sound. We took that idea and gave it a scientific job. Fire Jukebox is where harmonization meets sonification: a multisensory way to interpret one dataset, so a user can see the record, hear it and understand the difference between a real change and a sensor artifact. It does not sonify images and it does not add music to a dashboard. It is an alternative channel for the same scientific information.

This is our answer to a simple question: who gets to question Earth science data? A heat map answers nothing for a blind or low-vision analyst, and many learners understand pattern better by ear. Making the record audible widens the circle of people who can examine it, including researchers, teachers, students and inclusive classrooms.

The mapping is mathematical and fixed. With a count n and a series maximum n_max, we place the value on a logarithmic scale,

t = log(1 + n) / log(1 + n_max), t between 0 and 1

because we hear pitch in ratios and fire counts span orders of magnitude. In Sensor Jump the pitch is continuous,

f = 130.8 · 2^(3t) Hz

which spans three octaves, so doubling a count raises the pitch by a fixed musical interval and the size of a jump is audible. The record is played twice, first as the raw MODIS-then-VIIRS stitch and then harmonized, so the leap appears in the first pass and is gone in the second. In Fire Season Melody each year gives twelve notes, one per month, quantized to a C-major pentatonic scale from C3 to C6, louder and brighter when a month is above the area's median and softer and darker below, so a fire season is heard as a rise and fall. In Decades Sweep each year is one note across the whole record, about thirty seconds in total. In the daily view a crackle whose click rate follows the day's count conveys density.

All sound is computed live in the browser with the Web Audio API. No audio model and no sample library are used, and no AI generates any audio. Nothing autoplays, the default volume is low, Stop always works, and every mode has a text description and live caption. Sonification makes patterns perceivable. It does not validate the harmonization, which rests on the cross-validation above.

BEYOND THE FUNDAMENTAL CHALLENGE

The challenge asks for MODIS and VIIRS hotspots to be harmonized, for comparison across instruments over time, and for a burning activity calendar. KELVIN is built on NASA FIRMS and its resources: MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections from five satellites, in science-quality and near-real-time processing; the FIRMS Area API, MAP_KEY, Data Availability API and Archive Download; and NASA's MODIS and VIIRS documentation, including the VIIRS 375 m user guide. On that base it delivers an uncertainty-aware harmonization, a continuous series from November 2000, and an accessible calendar with ranking, seasons and trends. It goes further with data-reliability screening, a validation framework, a path for future sensors, and sound.

Its uses follow from that continuity. Environmental researchers get a documented, versioned series to build on and challenge. Agricultural fire management teams can judge whether a burning season differs from earlier ones without being misled by the instrument. Disaster-preparedness and forest-management teams get season windows, record months and early-season signals for any area they draw. Climate studies get a long record that does not break at instrument changes. Teachers and students get a hands-on lesson in why instruments change data and what calibration does, in a form that blind learners can use too.

WHAT IS DONE, WHAT IS SHOWN, AND WHAT COMES NEXT

We state this plainly. Implemented and tested: the FIRMS client, cleaning and rule-based screening, the global 1 km grid, calibration with shrinkage and bootstrap, the Terra-only correction, leave-one-year-out validation, the analytics, the API, and the interface with Fire Jukebox. Demonstrated with real NASA FIRMS data: our first regions, which are demonstration and validation cases only. Described here but still being extended and tested: the mathematical screening score, the wider Asian, Indo-Pacific and California analyses, and the early-warning indicators. We have not loaded the global archive, and we make no claim of validated prediction. A fresh copy of the repository starts with synthetic demonstration data that is not NASA observation data. Next come national and global tiles, a hosted public instance, validation of the screening score against independent records, a formal accessibility study, and correction factors that follow MODIS orbit drift after 2021. As an idea only, compatible fire observations from other space agencies could be added as further sensor families on the same cell-day grid, each calibrated on its overlap in the same way. We have not integrated or tested any non-NASA fire data. We will keep refining KELVIN through expert discussion, beginning with what we learned from specialists at ISRO's Space Applications Centre.

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

A hotspot is a thermal anomaly in a pixel, not an individual fire, a burned area, a cause or an exact temperature. One fire can fill many cells, and several can share one. Clouds, smoke and overpass timing limit every polar-orbiting sensor, and scaling corrects the average difference between sensors, not individual small fires. Terra-only months are estimated.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, DuckDB with Parquet, pandas, NumPy, SciPy and Shapely on the back end. React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts, d3 and the Web Audio API on the front end. Esri and OpenStreetMap basemaps, and Nominatim for place search. Every harmonization carries a version label (kelvin-h1.0) and all settings sit in a single configuration file, so any result can be reproduced.

WHY KELVIN SHOULD EXIST

Satellites will keep improving, and each improvement will quietly cut the record in two unless someone stitches it back together with care. KELVIN is not only about observing where Earth burns. It is about keeping that knowledge continuous, being honest about how reliable it is, and letting everyone, whether they read a chart or listen to it, ask whether a fire season is unusual.
